title: Irony Squared
author: Kirschner, Paul
summary: Paul Kirschner reflects on Rose Horowitch's Atlantic essay 'The End of Reading Is Here,' finding deep irony in a long, demanding piece about literacy decline—published in a format few post-literate readers will complete. A text-to-speech button converts the article into an oral, transient medium, and social media summaries reduce it to image-based memes. The essay perfectly illustrates what it laments: the narrowing audience for sustained written thought.
points: Horowitch's Atlantic essay on reading decline is itself a long, inference-heavy longread that speaks only to the literate minority who can read it—preaching exclusively to the converted.
A text-to-speech option beneath the title converts the piece into oral media, removing the possibility of rereading and reflective pausing that distinguish deep reading from passive listening.
NYT bestsellers now have sentences about one-third shorter than a century ago; even mainstream literary culture has adapted downward in complexity to serve a shrinking attentive readership.
Social media summaries of the article consist largely of image-based memes with minimal text, demonstrating the very post-literate trends the article describes.
The people who can read and benefit from Horowitch's essay form a cultural subculture; the article reaches those who already agree and cannot reach those who most need its argument.
A society losing deep reading loses the cognitive infrastructure for inference, cross-reference, and sustained intellectual attention that complex thought requires.
quotes: Being able to listen to the text, amongst other things, makes the text oral and, thus, allows the you – now the listener and not the reader - to do other things while listening to it removing the possibility of thinking about it while listening because our attention is limited and the possibility to reread passages and think about them is lost due to orality’s ethereal nature (i.e., once said it floats away into the ether; it is transitive).

It’s full of references both to what has earlier been said in the article as well as to history, psychological and media research forcing the reader to think and make inferences, those things that it also argues that we have and are becoming less able to do, namely read long and intricate sentences in large pieces of text.

In essence it’s a saunter through the history of literacy beginning with the Library of Alexandria through artificial intelligence, the role and function of reading and writing for our thinking our brain and society in general, and the effects of our loss of literacy in what is called the post-literate society.

Horowitch writes, “New York Times best sellers today have sentences that are about one-third shorter than they were a century ago.” In 1958, the English translation of Boris Pasternak’s Doctor Zhivago was the best-selling novel of the year, according to Publishers Weekly.

Whatever the book’s pleasures, it isn’t Pasternak: “A muscle in his square jaw ticks as he stares down at me, rippling the tawny-brown skin of his stubbled cheek.” In that respect it’s preaching to the converted, something I also often tend yo do.
